We will consider the function $T:\real^2\to\real^2$ that rotates a vector $\xvec$ by $45^\circ$ in the counterclockwise direction to obtain $T(\xvec)$ as seen in [fig-45-rotation].

The function $T$ rotates a vector counterclockwise by $45^\circ$.

We first need to know that $T$ can be represented by a matrix transformation, which means, by [prop-linear-trans-characterization], that we need to verify the linearity properties: $$ \begin{aligned} T(c\vvec) \amp {}={} cT(\vvec) \\ T(\vvec + \wvec) \amp {}={} T(\vvec) + T(\wvec)\text{.} \end{aligned} $$

The next two figures illustrate why these properties hold. For instance, [fig-45-rotation-linear-mult] shows the relationship between $T(\vvec)$ and $T(c\vvec)$ when $c$ is a scalar. In particular, scaling a vector and then rotating it is the same as rotating and then scaling it, which means that $T(c\vvec) = cT(\vvec)$.

We see that the vector $T(c\vvec)$ is a scalar multiple to $T(\vvec)$ so that $T(c\vvec) = cT(\vvec)$.

Similarly, [fig-45-rotation-linear-add] shows the relationship between $T(\vvec+\wvec)$, $T(\vvec)$, and $T(\wvec)$. Remember that the sum of two vectors is represented by the diagonal of the parallelogram defined by the two vectors. The rotation $T$ has the effect of rotating the parallelogram defined by $\vvec$ and $\wvec$ into the parallelogram defined by $T(\vvec)$ and $T(\wvec)$, explaining why $T(\vvec+\wvec) = T(\vvec) + T(\wvec)$.

We see that the vector $T(\vvec+\wvec)$ is the sum of $T(\vvec)$ and $T(\wvec)$ so that $T(\vvec + \wvec) = T(\vvec) + T(\wvec)$.

Having verified these two properties, we now know that the function $T$ that rotates vectors by $45^\circ$ is a matrix transformation. We may therefore write it as $T(\xvec) = A\xvec$ where $A$ is the $2\times2$ matrix $A=\left[\begin{array}{rr} T(\evec_1) \amp T(\evec_2) \end{array}\right]$. The columns of this matrix, $T(\evec_1)$ and $T(\evec_2)$, are shown on the right of [fig-45-rotation-basis].

The matrix transformation $T$ rotates $\evec_1$ and $\evec_2$ by $45^\circ$.

Notice that $T(\evec_1)$ forms an isosceles right triangle, as shown in [fig-45-rotation-e1]. Since the length of $\evec_1$ is 1, the length of $T(\evec_1)$, the hypotenuse of the triangle, is also 1, and by Pythagoras' theorem, the lengths of its legs are $1/\sqrt{2}$.

The vector $T(\evec_1)$ has length 1 and is the hypotenuse of a right isosceles triangle.

This leads to $T(\evec_1) = \twovec{\frac1{\sqrt{2}}} {\frac1{\sqrt{2}}}$. In the same way, we find that $T(\evec_2) = \twovec{-\frac1{\sqrt{2}}} {\frac1{\sqrt{2}}}$ so that the matrix $A$ is $$ A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \amp -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \amp \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \end{array}\right] $$ . You may wish to check this using the interactive diagram in the previous activity using the approximation $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.7$.
